title: Electrical Work — Fire System Wiring, Panels, Batteries and Mains Supply
verdict:
Close, but no. I would not sign this one yet, and the reason is small and fixable.

WHAT IS RIGHT, AND IT IS MOST OF IT. I rebuilt the shipping version (11 steps) and checked the shape: all twelve content keys, id unchanged, six-key steps, controls in hierarchy order in every step, residual never above initial, no step with only administrative and PPE controls claiming LOW, hrcw clause well formed, and the Electrical Safety Regulation 2013 (Qld) named once and only alongside the 2026 replacement. Then I pulled the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) SL 2026 No. 113 and the Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) SL 2008 No. 160 off legislation.qld.gov.au and read the sections. Every citation that changed is right, in its words. ES Reg 2026 s 199(2)(a) really does have two cumulative limbs — "(i) the work is to be performed on the supply side of the main switch ... and (ii) the point at which the equipment can be disconnected ... is not reasonably accessible from the work location" — and steps[8].controls[8] now states both. WHS Reg s 529A defines processing exactly as quoted and puts concrete, brick, tile, grout, mortar and render outside "engineered stone"; s 529B(3) does name AS/NZS 1716:2012 and AS/NZS 1715:2009; s 529C is 60 penalty units; s 529CA(3) forbids regard to PPE or administrative controls; s 529CD(2) is the 5-year record. s 78(3) is "on the ground or on a solid construction"; s 79(3)(a) and (5) are the fall prevention device and the working platform. s 208(3)(a), s 208(5)(b), s 209 and s 210(1)(d) all say what the pumpset controls claim. BFSR s 53 puts the 24-hour critical defect notice on the person who carried out the maintenance at 30 penalty units, and s 49 gives both worked examples verbatim. The two fatal findings from last round — silica and the diesel pumpset — are not gestured at, they are properly done: coupling, starting batteries, VSD DC bus, exhaust flue, carbon monoxide, hot manifold, all with a stop-work. The re-rating is honest and the levelling is fixed.

WHY IT STILL FAILS. steps[4] is the step this crew does most, the document itself calls it energised electrical work, and its sixteen controls never once require a safety observer or the rescue kit. The observer is in the "responsible" string only — which is the exact fault the last round found at steps[8] and fixed there. ES Reg 2026 s 203(1)(c) makes the observer mandatory; s 203(3) does not help, because working inside a panel is not "only testing". Second, steps[2].controls[3] now orders a technician to open and lock the isolator at the array — that is a roof — and steps[2] carries no fall hazard, no access control, and no pointer to the heights SWMS, and it is not one of the three steps the whenRequired section says carries the access controls. Third, steps[6] triggers its stop on cell TYPE and never on cell CONDITION: a VRLA bank cooked by a failed charger is the most common way this trade meets hydrogen, and a failing charger is why the tech was called.

Fix those three and the minors below and I would sign it without argument.

WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY. I did not reach a standards source, so I am not certifying any AS or AS/NZS edition — AS 1851, AS 1670.1/.4, AS/NZS 3000, AS/NZS 3017, AS 2941, AS 3011, AS 2676, AS IEC 60900, AS 1892, AS/NZS 5033, AS/NZS 5139. The document cites them by designation without years and tells the reader to confirm, which is the right posture, so I raise no finding on them. I also did not confirm the current titles of the Queensland codes of practice.

blocking.field: steps[4] ("Open the fire indicator panel and work inside it") — controls[] has no safety observer control and no rescue-gear control; the observer appears only in steps[4].responsible
blocking.problem: steps[4].controls[6] says in its own words that "Opening a panel with the mains terminal block, transformer or charger exposed IS energised electrical work", and steps[4].hazards[4] says "Anyone standing within 3 m of the exposed mains block, transformer or charger is in energised electrical work". Sixteen controls follow and not one of them requires a safety observer to be present and observing. I checked: no control in steps[4] contains the word "observer" or the word "rescue". The observer is named only in steps[4].responsible ("Licensed electrical worker with a safety observer where any part inside the cabinet is energised"), which is who does the step, not a control on it. Verified against legislation.qld.gov.au: Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 203(1) requires electrical work on or near energised electrical equipment to be performed "(c) subject to subsection (3), observed by a safety observer", and the only relief, s 203(3), is where "(a) the work consists only of testing; and (b) a risk assessment conducted under section 199(1)(a) shows there is no serious risk". Working inside an open FIP with the mains block, transformer and charger live is not work consisting only of testing. This is the same fault the previous round identified at steps[8] and repaired there — steps[8].controls[9] now carries a full observer control — while steps[4] was left as it was. steps[5] also lays out the rescue gear at the panel (steps[5].controls[12]: insulated rescue hook, first aid kit, vehicle AED, phone with signal confirmed) and forbids walking away from a live open panel (steps[5].controls[13]); steps[4] carries neither. steps[0].controls[5] does require "Two people on site whenever a panel is opened with 240 V present" and says the second person must meet the observer definition for energised work — but two people on site is not an observer observing. On a real job the second person walks off to the switchboard or to test detectors, and the step that governs the work says nothing to stop that.
blocking.fix: Add an administrative control to steps[4], worded to match steps[5].controls[11]: wherever the mains terminal block, transformer or charger is exposed, a safety observer meeting the schedule 10 definition observes the work and does nothing else — no handing tools, no paperwork, no phone; the only relief is Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 203(3), and it does not cover working inside an open panel. Add a second administrative control mirroring steps[5].controls[12]: rescue hook or dry timber, first aid kit, vehicle AED and a phone with signal confirmed standing at that spot, laid out where the observer can reach them before the door opens. Add steps[5].controls[13] as well — the panel does not get left open and unattended, door shut and locked if you step out. Place all three below the isolate and engineering controls.

blocking.field: steps[2].controls[3] ("Solar PV and battery storage do not die when you open a breaker...") — steps[2].hazards[] carries no fall hazard and steps[2].controls[] carries no access control; siteSpecificPrompts[9]
blocking.problem: The PV correction is good electrically and it introduces a task the document never controls. steps[2].controls[3] is an isolate-level, mandatory instruction: "Open the PV AC breaker at the board, then open and lock the DC isolator at the inverter AND the isolator at the array." On a commercial building the array isolator is on the roof. steps[2] names four hazards, all electrical, and eight controls, none about access. The word "roof" appears three times in the whole statement — "rooftop solar" in a phone call, "roof space" in a heat control, and "Look up at the roof" in a prompt — and never once about standing on one. Worse, the whenRequired section tells the reader exactly which steps carry the access controls: "it is covered by THIS statement — the access controls in the panel step, the energised testing step and the cable step". steps[2] is not one of them. siteSpecificPrompts[9] asks how you will reach "each panel, rack, cable tray and detector base" and never mentions the roof or the array. So the statement creates a rooftop task inside a control the crew cannot skip, and then says nothing about edge protection, anchor points, roof access, fragile roofing, skylights, or the fact that a fall of more than 2 m is separate high risk construction work needing the heights SWMS.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[2].hazards: "Getting to a rooftop PV array isolator — unprotected roof edge, fragile roof sheeting and skylights, ladder access to roof level." Add an administrative control to steps[2]: the array DC isolator is only approached once roof access has been planned — safe means of access, edge protection or an anchored system, no work on a fragile or wet roof, nobody on the roof alone — and where the access is a fall of more than 2 m that is separate high risk construction work under Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 291(a) and it goes to the heights SWMS before anybody goes up. If roof access cannot be made safe today, the board is not treated as isolated and the work is done live under steps[5] or it does not start. Add to siteSpecificPrompts[9] or as a new prompt: "If the board carries PV, where is the array isolator, how do you get to it, what is the roof made of, and is there edge protection or an anchor point?" Amend the whenRequired sentence listing which steps hold the access controls so it names the isolation step too.

blocking.field: steps[6] ("Replace the battery bank") — hazards[] and controls[0]
blocking.problem: The step's stop trigger is the wrong variable. steps[6].controls[0] reads "Identify the cell type before you touch anything. If the bank is vented (flooded) cells, or it sits in a dedicated battery room, STOP." That catches cell type and location and misses cell condition. The word hydrogen appears twice in the whole document, both times about vented cells. Nothing anywhere names a sealed VRLA bank that is already faulty — swollen or bulged cases, cells hot to the back of the hand, a case split and weeping, a cabinet that smells sour, a charger stuck in boost. That is thermal runaway, and a VRLA in thermal runaway vents hydrogen through its relief valves into a closed FIP battery cabinet exactly as a vented cell does. The crew is standing there because the panel is showing a battery or charger fault, so a failed charger cooking the bank is not the unlikely case, it is the referral. steps[6].hazards[0] concedes "a 24 V bank will deliver hundreds of amps into a dead short", so the ignition source is already in the step: the first spark is the terminal nut the technician is about to break. steps[6].controls[6] deals with how a bank is installed and ventilated, not with a bank that is gassing in front of you right now, and steps[6].residualRisk "high" does not cover a hazard the step never names.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[6].hazards: "A sealed VRLA bank already in thermal runaway — swollen or split cases, cells hot to touch, a charger stuck in boost. Sealed cells vent hydrogen too when they are cooking, and the cabinet is closed." Add a stop to steps[6].controls[0], or a second eliminate control immediately after it: before anything is disconnected, look at and feel the bank — if any cell is swollen, split, weeping, hot, or the charger is in permanent boost, STOP. Do not break a terminal, do not switch anything in that cabinet. Open the cabinet or the room and leave it to ventilate with nobody in front of it, isolate the charger supply at the board from outside the cabinet if you can reach it, and ring the office. That bank is a flammable atmosphere and it goes to the flammable atmosphere SWMS the same as vented cells. Add to siteSpecificPrompts[14], after the sealed-or-vented question: "What condition are the cells in — swollen, hot, split, weeping — and is the charger in boost?"

blocking.field: steps[7] ("Cable work — run, terminate and make good to the Wiring Rules") — hazards[]; steps[7].controls[6] is the only mention of sprinkler pipework in the document
blocking.problem: The crew is on a ladder with a drill, in the ceilings, risers and plant rooms of a building that is sprinklered — and the document never names the sprinkler installation as something in the room. The only mention anywhere is steps[7].controls[6], which forbids fixing fire-rated cable to sprinkler pipe: so the statement knows the pipework is there, and treats it only as a bad cable support. Nothing names knocking a head with a ladder, a cable draw or a length of conduit, or drilling into a wet pipe in a wall or ceiling. When a head goes, it discharges at pressure and it does not stop until somebody finds and shuts the control valve — into a space that on this job may hold an open fire indicator panel, an open switchboard, or a pump controller with the covers off. It also puts the brigade on the way to a building whose detection the same crew has just isolated, which the document handles nowhere.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[7].hazards: "Striking a sprinkler head or drilling a charged pipe while running cable — water at pressure into a room with an open panel or switchboard, and a brigade attendance on a system you have isolated." Add controls to steps[7]: administrative — look up and identify every head and every run of charged pipe before a ladder, a platform or a cable draw goes anywhere near them; nothing is rested against, tied to or used as support on sprinkler pipe; keep the drill and the ladder head clear of heads and pipe drops; before you start, find the sprinkler control valve, know who on site is authorised to shut it, and have their number. And an emergency line: if a head goes, get anybody clear of open live gear, shut the panel and the board if it is safe to reach, get the valve shut, ring 000 and the monitoring provider, and tell them the detection is already isolated.

blocking.field: whenRequired (the "SILICA — THIS STATEMENT IS THE PLAN" paragraph), permits[6], ppe[6], steps[7].hazards[3] and steps[7].controls[4] — the word "plasterboard"
blocking.problem: The chapter 8A reasoning is right for masonry and wrong for one item on the list. whenRequired says "Concrete, bricks, tiles, grout, mortar, render and plasterboard are expressly excluded from 'engineered stone' — which means they are NOT out of chapter 8A, they are ordinary crystalline silica substances". The first half is verbatim correct: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 529A, definition of engineered stone, paragraph (b), lists "(i) concrete products or cement products; (ii) bricks, pavers or other similar blocks; (iii) ceramic wall or floor tiles; (iv) grout, mortar or render; (v) plasterboard; (vi) porcelain products; (vii) sintered stone; (viii) roof tiles". The inference does not follow for plasterboard. Being outside "engineered stone" does not make a material a crystalline silica substance; s 529A sets a separate test — "material that contains at least 1% crystalline silica, determined as a weight/weight (w/w) concentration". Concrete, block, brick, mortar, render and tile clear that easily. Gypsum plasterboard generally does not. The statement then carries plasterboard through into duties it does not attract: permits[6] makes a written s 529CA assessment a stop before a powered hole in plasterboard, and steps[7].controls[4] requires H-class on-tool extraction "or with water suppression at the cut" on every powered hole into it. Water suppression into a plasterboard cut is not a thing anybody will do, and a rule the crew can see is silly is a rule they stop applying — including on the masonry next to it, where it is the difference between a job and silicosis.
blocking.fix: Drop "plasterboard" from the crystalline silica substance lists in permits[6], ppe[6], steps[7].hazards[3] and steps[7].controls[4], and from the inference sentence in the whenRequired silica paragraph — quote the s 529A exclusion list as it stands, then say that concrete, block, brick, mortar, render and tile clear the 1% test and are therefore crystalline silica substances. Keep siteSpecificPrompts[11] as it is: asking what the substrate actually is remains the right question. If Safe QLD wants extraction on plasterboard anyway, say so plainly as a company dust rule, not as a chapter 8A duty.

blocking.field: whenRequired — the "HOW RISK IS RATED IN THIS DOCUMENT" band definitions read against the new "AND THE FLOOR" paragraph and against steps[1], steps[7], steps[9] and steps[10] residualRisk "medium"
blocking.problem: The re-rating was done honestly and six steps went up, but the matrix underneath it still contradicts four of the ratings that stayed. The bands read: "EXTREME — catastrophic or major consequence at possible likelihood or higher ... HIGH — catastrophic or major consequence at unlikely likelihood or lower, or moderate at likely or higher; MEDIUM — moderate consequence at possible or lower, or minor at likely or higher". Between EXTREME and HIGH those two bands take every likelihood there is, so a catastrophic or major consequence has no MEDIUM cell at all, at any likelihood, and the paragraph then closes that door explicitly: "applying controls lowers LIKELIHOOD. It does not lower CONSEQUENCE." The consequence scale calls "an unprotected building that burns" catastrophic. On that reading steps[1] (hazards[0], no automatic brigade call), steps[7] (hazards[0] cutting a live cable, hazards[2] asbestos, hazards[3] silicosis), steps[9] (hazards[0] arc flash on energising, hazards[1] an enclosure live under fault) and steps[10] (hazards[0] closing the breaker on somebody's hands, hazards[6] the set cranking at the coupling, hazards[7] carbon monoxide, hazards[5] a client who thinks they are protected) all floor at HIGH, and all four are rated "medium". The new FLOOR paragraph does not reconcile this — it adds a narrower, worker-only rule naming four mechanisms ("an exposed live part, a busbar that cannot be isolated, a set that can start, a bank that can arc") beside the wider band definitions, so the document now carries two rules that disagree. It matters because the same paragraph instructs the reader to act on it: "If a residual rating in this document looks conveniently low to you, it is wrong and you raise it." A technician who does that raises four steps to HIGH, and the STOP WORK clause then sends handback, cable work and pre-energisation testing to the supervisor for authorisation — which is not what anybody intends and will teach the crew to ignore the gate that matters at steps[4], [5] and [8].
blocking.fix: Make the bands two-dimensional and finish the sentence. State that a residual retaining a catastrophic or major consequence sits at HIGH unless the remaining likelihood is rare AND none of the FLOOR mechanisms is still present, in which case MEDIUM is available — then the four MEDIUM ratings stand on the page and the reader can reproduce them. Whichever way it is written, the FLOOR paragraph and the band definitions must give the same answer for steps[1], [7], [9] and [10], and the STOP WORK clause's list of what sits at HIGH must match the ratings actually in the steps.
